summary: End-to-end tests of the REST API through FastAPI's `TestClient` (the session-wide `client` fixture from `conftest.py`). They pin down the HTTP contract an integrating bank would rely on: what each status code means (201, 401, 404, 422), that ingestion normalizes, scores and explains, and that every read endpoint returns the shape the dashboard in `web/` expects. All tests share one seeded database, so they assert properties (counts above a floor, valid levels) rather than exact random values. The last two tests pin fixes from the code review: timestamp range checks, blank locations and malformed IDs.

notes.text: Docstring listing what this file covers: the API's public contract.

Imports the shared header and sample payload from `conftest.py`. This works because `pyproject.toml` adds `tests` to `pythonpath`; pytest has already imported conftest under that name, so the same module (and the same temp database) is reused.
Checks that the app seeded itself when the session's `client` started against an empty database (the lifespan hook in `iip/app.py`).
The seeder always creates exactly `USER_COUNT`, 25 customers.
Asks for up to 500 events but checks `total`, which counts every matching row regardless of page size. The fixed-seed data (about 476 events) comfortably clears the 300 floor.
The seeded attack scenarios must have produced at least one correlated incident.
Write endpoints are protected by `require_api_key`, part of the `WRITE` dependency list in `routes/deps.py`.
No `X-API-Key` header at all: rejected with 401 Unauthorized before the event is processed.
A wrong key is rejected the same way. The server compares keys with `secrets.compare_digest`, a constant-time comparison, so response timing can't reveal how much of a guess was right.
Shows that Pydantic (`schemas.EventIn`) rejects malformed input with 422 before it reaches the pipeline, while a well-formed but unknown reference gets 404.
`nope` isn't an IP address; the `_valid_ip` validator, built on Python's `ipaddress` module, rejects it.
`x` isn't one of the four allowed `event_type` values.
`bob` doesn't match the required `^USR-\d+$` pattern.

`USR-9999` passes validation (the shape is right), but no such customer exists: `process_event` raises `LookupError`, which the route turns into 404 Not Found. This separates a badly shaped request (422) from a valid request for a missing resource (404).
The main happy-path test: one event goes through normalization, scoring and storage.
Starts from `EVENT` and changes three things: a messy lowercase location padded with spaces, a device ID never seen before, and a suspicious IP reputation.
Posts with the valid key. A successful ingest answers 201 Created, set by `status_code=201` on the route.
Parses the JSON body, which holds `event` (the stored record), `risk` (the assessment) and `incident_id`.
The padded `london` was trimmed and mapped to the canonical label `London, UK`, proving normalization ran before storage.

`<=` on sets means is-a-subset-of: all three expected signals must be present, and others may appear too. DEV-7777 is unknown (New device), London isn't USR-1001's home city (Abu Dhabi in the seed data), and the reputation is suspicious (Suspicious IP).
Contributions are sorted heaviest first, so the top one must be Suspicious IP (+30). Impossible travel (+40) can't outrank it, because travel is never judged on a flagged IP.
Every response carries the headers added by `RequestContextMiddleware`: a request ID for tracing and the server-side processing time, formatted like `3.2ms`.
Reads the new event back by its public ID (such as `EVT-00477`) and checks the owner, proving the event was really stored and the ID format round-trips.
Unknown or malformed IDs must produce a clean 404, never a 500 crash.
Loops over four paths: an event ID that is well-formed but missing, a malformed one (`garbage`, which `parse_ref` turns into `None`), a missing incident and a missing user. Each must answer 404.
Tests the query parameters of `GET /api/v1/events`.
Filtering by level is case-insensitive (the route upper-cases `critical`): every returned item must be CRITICAL, and `limit=5` caps the page size.

Free-text search `q` also matches customer names: `fenwick` finds Ayla Fenwick, who is always USR-1001 because the seeder pairs the `FIRST` and `LAST` name lists in order. Every hit must belong to that customer.
`sort=asc` returns the oldest events first. Timestamps are ISO-8601 strings, which sort chronologically even when compared as plain text.
Fetches the customer list behind the Users page.
`dict.keys()` returns a set-like view, so `<=` checks that each user row carries the computed fields the dashboard needs.
Requests a profile with a lowercase ID (`usr-1004`); the route upper-cases it, and the profile must include devices and a risk history.
The current-risk endpoint must return one of the four valid levels. The exact level depends on seeded random activity, so the test checks the contract rather than a specific value.

Picks the first open incident (the route upper-cases `open`). The seeder always adds attacks from the last 15-120 minutes and only moves incidents older than a day out of OPEN, so an open one is guaranteed.
The detail view must include a timeline of correlated events, a generated title and a list of MITRE ATT&CK techniques.
Builds the incident's URL once for the three PATCH calls below.
Changing status is a write, so it needs the API key: without it, 401. The body is valid, so missing authentication is the only possible reason for failure.
With the key but an invalid status: 422, because `StatusIn` only allows OPEN, INVESTIGATING or RESOLVED. Each of these calls isolates exactly one failure mode.
A valid transition succeeds, and the response already reflects the new status.
Fetches the aggregate payload behind the Overview screen.
Events exist, and there is exactly one bucket per day for the last seven days.
24 hourly buckets for the last day, and 21 histogram buckets for scores 0, 5, 10 ... 100. Every weight is a multiple of 5, so every possible score lands on one of those buckets.
The threat map needs coordinates: cities must be present and each must carry `lat` (cities without coordinates are skipped by `geo_overview`).
The rulebook endpoint lists every signal (11 today); `>= 10` tolerates future additions.

The what-if scorer returns 45 for New device + Suspicious IP, the same number `test_rules.py` gets from the engine directly, showing the API runs the same code. No key is needed because this dry run stores nothing.
Unknown signal names are rejected with 422 by `EvaluateIn`'s validator before they reach the engine.
Fetches the integration health endpoint.
`CONNECTED` means the database answered a `select 1`. `deterministic` proves that `conftest.py` really removed `OPENAI_API_KEY`, so no test can reach the real OpenAI API.
Collects every path with at least one operation that needs the key. The catalog is generated from the OpenAPI schema, where `require_api_key` shows up as an `x-api-key` header parameter.
Both ingestion and incident triage must be listed as secured. If someone removed `WRITE` from either route, this assertion would catch it.
The metrics endpoint must have counted requests (the global counter includes every API call made so far in the session) and must return a 30-minute throughput series, one value per minute.
Fetches the dashboard page served at `/`.
The page loads, and because `IIP_DEMO_MODE` defaults to true, the server replaced the `__IIP_API_KEY__` placeholder in `index.html` with the real key (`test-key`), as the inline comment says.
FastAPI's automatic Swagger UI at `/docs` must be available.
The favicon route serves the SVG icon, so browsers don't log a 404 for it.
Timestamps the engine can't use are rejected with a 422, never accepted.
A far-future date (which would keep the customer's incident open to every later event), a year-1 date with an offset (which used to overflow into a 500) and a date before 2000 are all refused.
Client mistakes stay client errors: a location of only spaces is now trimmed before the length check, so it fails validation instead of being stored empty.
A superscript digit (which `isdigit()` accepts but `int()` rejects) and a 20-digit number (which overflows SQLite) are a plain 404, not a server error.
